title: Most Crowded Digit-Sum Groups
statement:
Take the integers from 1 to n and put two numbers in the same group when their digit sums are equal. For example, 7, 16 and 25 all have digit sum 7, so they share a group.

Some groups end up larger than others. Return how many groups share the largest size (not the size itself).

examples.why: Groups {1, 10}, {2, 11} and {3, 12} have 2 members each; the digit sums 4 to 9 have one member each. Three groups tie for the largest size.
Every number is alone in its group, so all 5 groups tie at size 1.
Digit sum 2 now holds {2, 11, 20}, three members. It is the only group of that size.

hints: You never need the members of a group, only how many there are. What should the map count?
The digit sum of any number up to a million is at most 54, so an array of 55 counters is enough.
Count sizes, find the maximum size, then count how many groups have exactly that size.

explain.intuition:
The groups are keyed by digit sum, so a counter per digit sum is all you need: walk 1 to n, compute each digit sum, and bump its counter. Then the question is two simple passes over the counters: what is the largest count, and how many counters equal it.

A small trick speeds up the digit sums: the digit sum of i is the digit sum of floor(i / 10) plus i % 10, and you have already computed the first part. That makes each number O(1).
steps: Create a counter array size indexed by digit sum.
For each i from 1 to n, compute its digit sum and increment size[sum].
Return how many entries of size equal best.
pitfalls: Returning the largest group size instead of the number of groups with that size.
Sizing a counter array for small n only. Digit sums grow with the number of digits: 999 999 has digit sum 54.
Starting from 0 instead of 1, which adds a fake group for digit sum 0.

complexity.time: O(n) with the reuse trick, O(n log n) recomputing digits
complexity.space: O(n) for the reuse table, otherwise O(1)

solutions.title: Count with a map
solutions.idea: Compute each digit sum by peeling digits and tally group sizes in a map.

solutions.title: Reuse earlier digit sums
solutions.idea: digitSum(i) = digitSum(floor(i / 10)) + i % 10, so each digit sum costs O(1) with a table.

followups: n goes up to 10¹⁸. How would you count numbers per digit sum without visiting each one?
Return the members of the largest groups in increasing order.
